The process can be fraught with difficulties hearing, speaking or comprehending, which may result in breakdown in communication among interlocutors. One accessible conversation mechanism for resolving trouble sources is through the employment of repair initiation (Atar & Seedhouse, 2018). This study investigates the nature and function of repair initiation in Ghanaian ESL classrooms by qualitatively analysing 52 hours of recordings of ESL classroom interactions. The data is examined focusing explicitly on the repair initiation mechanism. Results from this study provide a discovery of verbal and non-verbal repair initiations as a resource to clarify conversation breakdown. These insights offer empirical contributions to the literature on L2 interactional competence and classroom discourse. Furthermore, the study underscores the pedagogical relevance of repair ARTICLE IN PRESS mechanisms, highlighting the need for teacher professional development programs to include explicit training on managing communication breakdowns in ESL settings. Keywords: Classroom Interaction; Conversation Analysis; English as a Second Language; Repair Initiation Introduction Language plays a fundamental role in interaction, especially in the ESL classroom. Whenever there are effective interactions, the learning of the target language is propelled (Estaji & Rajabi, 2019). Hence, in ESL classroom interactions, when troubles occur in understanding others' turn, speakers must employ a range of communicative strategies to signal troubles and confirm their comprehension more explicitly (Aleksius, 2021). Thus, interlocutors should be able to use the target sounds and speak intelligibly to facilitate the understanding of the message and repair when S the conversation breaks down (Atar & Seedhouse, 2018). Repair, according to Liddicoat (2022), S is a mechanism that operates in conversation to deal with problems in speaking, hearing, and E understanding in talk-in-interaction. Scholars such as Jefferson (2018), Atar and Seedhouse R (2018), Mozaffari et al. (2018), Sert & Balaman (2018), and Aleksius (2021) have contributed significantly to this body of knowledge by examiningP various aspects of repair initiation practices in discourse. For example, Atar and Seedhou se (2018) analysed teacher-initiated repair N mechanisms, highlighting the diverse strategies employed to prompt and guide repair sequences. I Mozaffari et al. (2018) also delved into language teachers’ repair initiation practices, shedding light on their implications for learning oEutcomes. Meanwhile, Sert and Balaman (2018) focused on students’ repair mechanisms, tracing the evolution from reliance on external repairs to the L development of self-repair strategiCes. I This study is propelled by a dual motivation: the extensive focus on repair initiation studies within T the realm of English language discourse (Kendrick, 2015), juxtaposed against the dearth of studies R into repair initiation in second language classrooms in Ghana. While existing research generally A outlines a sequence of trouble turn, initiation turn, and repair turn, it falls short of asserting the universality of repair initiation practices, particularly in the context of second language acquisition and learning (Aleksius, 2021; Bostrom, 2021; Dingemanse & Enfield, 2015; Lutzenberger et al., 2024; Obeng, & Campbell, 2024). Against this backdrop, the current study examines how Ghanaian ESL teachers and students navigate the complexities of repair initiation. The scarcity of research on repair initiation in ESL contexts such as Ghana underscores the significance of this study. The following research questions guide the study: 1) What repair initiations do teachers and students employ in ESL classroom discourse? and 2) What are the functions of the repair initiation strategies teachers and students employ in the interaction? The rationale behind the conduct of this enquiry is three-fold: First, the results of the study reveals what teachers of English language can learn about how communication with their students is shaped by looking at the details of their interactions. Second, as the first study on repair initiation practices in ESL classrooms in Ghana, the findings might also reveal how educators foster or stifle learning possibilities during interactions. In the end, raising teachers’ linguistic awareness will lead to an improvement in classroom behaviour. Third, this study also has another component that might be helpful for teacher-researchers who want to conduct a study but are unsure of how to analyse their data. The instructor-researcher may encounter two distinct obstacles in terms of data ARTICLE IN PRESS and data analysis. Regarding students, it could serve as a reflection for them of how conversational impediments are handled. This study advances CA by exploring repair initiation in a non-Western ESL context, challenging the notion that repair mechanisms are universal. Using data from Ghanaian classrooms, it demonstrates how sociolinguistic and cultural factors influence communication and repair practices. Contextually, it represents the first systematic examination of repair initiation in Ghana’s ESL classrooms, offering insights that enrich understanding of interactional competence and inform teacher training, classroom discourse, and cross-cultural communication. 2. Literature Review 2.1 Repair initiations Repair initiation serves as a pivotal moment in discourse, wherein a speaker acknowledges and seeks resolution for a preceding turn perceived to contain a problem (Jan & Saad, 2018). This S initiation sets in motion a dynamic interplay between speakers, where the one who produced the S trouble source offers repair afterwards. To navigate this intricate process effectively, speakers must E possess a repertoire of linguistic, cognitive, and social skills (Aleksius, 2021). Dingemanse and R Enfield (2015) underscore the interconnectedness of language, cognition, and social dynamics P inherent in repair initiation, emphasising how these skills facilitate the organisation of repair initiation sequences to address occurring troubles swiftly. Central to this process is the design of N an initiation turn that succinctly communicates the nature of the breakdown to the co-speaker I (Hayashi & Kim, 2015). Consequently, spe akers are expected to adeptly utilise various linguistic E resources to craft initiation turns that effectively convey the nature of the problem (Dingemanse, L 2015). C Repair initiations come in two tIypes: verbal and nonverbal initiations (Atar & Seedhouse, 2018). Verbal repair initiation typicaTlly occurs in three basic formats: restricted request, restricted offer, R and open request (Dingemanse & Enfield, 2015). Restricted request repair initiations highlight the trouble source of the pArevious turn, often using question words or partial repetition to single out the trouble source. Open request repair initiation, on the other hand, does not identify a trouble source but addresses the entire previous turn. According to Clift (2016), Open request repair initiation can appear in various forms, such as interjections like "Huh?" set phrases like "Sorry?" or more complete questions like "What did you say?" For the purposes of this study, we focus on restricted request and open request Open-class repair initiation is a flexible strategy used when the trouble source in the prior turn is unspecified, often due to hearing issues or misunderstandings (Wong & Waring, 2010). This has been studied across languages like Icelandic (Dehé, 2015), German, French, Japanese, and Korean (Duran, et al., 2019; Golato & Golato, 2015; Hayashi & Kim, 2015) and among Iranian EFL learners (Fotovatnia & Dorri, 2013). This approach frequently involves interrogative pronouns (e.g., "what"), interjections (e.g., "huh"), or affirmatives (e.g., "yeah"), either alone or with other repair techniques like repetition, to address various communicative difficulties (Enfield et al., 2013). ARTICLE IN PRESS Repetition is a common repair initiation strategy that involves reiterating elements from the trouble source with rising intonation to signal uncertainty and prompt the speaker to complete the repair (Aleksius, 2021). This technique not only seeks clarification but also conveys emotions like astonishment or disbelief, enhancing comprehension (Kaur, 2020). Research shows that repetition effectively addresses comprehension issues, requests clarification, seeks confirmation, and aids learners in identifying trouble sources (Persson, 2015; Wang & Wu, 2015). Similarly, candidate understanding involves paraphrasing to demonstrate comprehension and assist in formulating clearer utterances, often used in Other-Initiated Repair (OIR) to address immediate conversational issues (Atar & Seedhouse, 2018; Kendrick, 2015). Nonverbal repair initiation is often expressed through gestures, head movements, eye contact, facial expressions (such as smiling), bodily postures, and symbolic actions, which frequently accompany verbal discourse, whether intentionally or unintentionally. As Negi (2009) observes, nonverbal communication performs several key functions, including substituting, complementing, regulating, and even contradicting verbal messages. In recentS years, the role of nonverbal communication in ESL classrooms has attracted increasing scSholarly attention, particularly with the rise of interest in multimodality within second langEuage instruction (Atar et al., 2020; Mortensen, 2016; Rasmussen, 2014; Sert, 2017). For inRstance, Rasmussen (2014) examined the act of leaning forward, revealing that this behaviour, when combined with verbal utterances, P contributes to more effective interaction. Her findings demonstrated that leaning forward is frequently employed during repair turns. SimNilarly, Balaman (2017) found that teachers in preschool contexts employed leaning forward as part of a broader repertoire of resources including I crouching, shifting posture, walking toward students, and cupping a hand behind the ear to elicit E student responses and facilitate interaction. L 2.2 Theoretical Framework C I This study is conducted within the framework of Conversation Analysis CA), as pioneered by T Garfinkel (1967). The principles and methodologies of CA have been elaborated upon in the R seminal works of Sacks (1984), Sacks et al. (1974), Drew and Heritage (2006), Heritage and A Clayman (2010), and Heritage (2012). CA focuses on the intricate ways in which members of a social group or society collectively construct and navigate social and interactional situations, as well as the social actions and interactions they engage in within those contexts. Practitioners of CA employ inductive and rigorous methods to analyse the techniques that individuals use to make sense of and participate in their social environments, mainly through talk-in-interaction (Liddicoat, 2022). In this study, we utilise CA to examine how participants in an ESL classroom initiate repair during interactions. We investigate how the ESL classroom context either facilitates or hinders repair initiations. Specifically, we focus on various types of repair initiation, both verbal and nonverbal, and the methods by which these interruptions are managed and resolved. Our analysis emphasises the detailed examination of transcribed recorded data, looking for recurring patterns and practices in the interactions. By focusing on these elements, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of how repairs are initiated in ESL classrooms. This focus involves a close examination of the conversational techniques used by learners to initiate repair and the role of the classroom environment in supporting or obstructing these processes. Particular attention is given to how teachers and students respond to each initiate repair, through turn-taking or interruptions. ARTICLE IN PRESS Methods and Material 3.1 Context of the Study The data was collected from ESL classrooms in Senior High Schools in the Upper East Region of Ghana. The Upper East Region is one of the administrative regions of Ghana. It is divided into fifteen administrative districts. The region has thirty-six public-funded senior high schools/technical institutes in different districts established to satisfy the people’s pre-tertiary education needs. In Ghana, Senior High School marks the second level of education, where English language learning focuses on refining students’ language skills and competencies, boosting their confidence and communicative abilities, and fostering a love for reading for pleasure. It also aims to nurture creativity, enhance proficiency in English, and enable effective communication with other English speakers. ESL lessons are generally teacher-led, with educators designing activities that actively engage students and promote maximum participation. The objective of English language instruction at the Senior High School level in Ghana, where the data for this study was collected, is to enhance students’ language competencies, preparSing them to function effectively in professional environments and to progress to tertiary educatiSon. This study focused on discourse within English language classrooms, with audio recordEings of lessons conducted between September 2022 and March 2023. R 3.2 Research Design P Classroom ethnography design was utilisedN for this enquiry (Brewer, 2000). Classroom ethnography specifically targets micro-level dIynamics within the classroom environment (Hassen & Mekbib, 2021). It closely examines the detailed interactions between teachers and students, E focusing on the discourse, behaviours, and routines that structure classroom culture (Brewer, L 2000). This approach explores elements such as student engagement, classroom repair practices, C teacher-student relationships, and the implicit hidden curriculum conveyed through classroom I routines (Hassen & Mekbib, 2021). This study took place in twenty-six ESL classrooms in the T Upper East Region of Ghana using the following research questions: 1) What repair initiation R strategies do teachers and students employ in ESL classroom interaction? 2) What are the functions A of these repair initiation strategies in ESL classroom interaction? The pragmatic paradigm shaped the study (Sarantakos, 2012), aiding the researchers in gaining a collective insight into conversation initiation practices in the ESL classroom in the Upper East Region of Ghana. 3.3 Participants and Sampling The population was all ESL classrooms in the Upper East Region of Ghana. The target population for this study consists of all ESL classrooms of senior high schools in the Upper East Region, including Forms 1, 2, and 3. Since the study is about Repair initiation practices in the ESL classroom, the researchers considered it appropriate to involve only teachers and students. In all, 52 hours of ESL classroom lessons were recorded with 10 lessons observed. Approximately 1,283 students participated across the recorded and observed classes, with an average class size of 35 students in a class. The students represented an upper-intermediate proficiency level based on internal school assessments and national examination performance. The sample thus reflects typical upper-intermediate language abilities found in Ghanaian senior high schools. 3.4 Procedure and Data Collection ARTICLE IN PRESS The researchers meticulously followed appropriate ethical procedures to obtain clearance and approval for this study. Two research assistants were recruited to undergo training to facilitate the data collection and transcription processes. Including these assistants was deemed necessary due to the extended time required not only for waiting during lessons but also for covering the 28 chosen senior high schools within the designated research timeframe. Functioning as non- participant observers alongside the researchers, they strategically positioned themselves to take notes during ESL lessons while minimising potential disruption. Both research assistants were graduate students from the University of Education, Winneba, specialising in Applied Linguistics. Consequently, their graduate studies equipped them with ample exposure to discourse analysis methods. They were provided them with training on using a Casio V6 digital audio recorder for data recording, observing relevant non-verbal features, and taking notes on significant non-verbal information crucial for data analysis. Post-sessions, a collaborative effort between the researchers and the assistants, involved comparing and transcribing notes to enhance transcription quality. 3.5 Data Analysis Techniques S CA procedure was used for the data analysis. CA can be uSnderstood as a distinct analytical framework that provides insights into how individuals engage in social interaction through E conversation (Liddicoat, 2022). Data for CA must consist of authentic talk occurring in naturalistic R settings (Hutchby, 2019), as CA focuses explicitly on analysing context-bound, real-world P interactions. Given that CA’s analytical system is designed to illuminate the sequential features of talk, the researchers examined adjacency pairsN as they emerged in the discourse from an emic perspective. The process involved identifying repair practices in accordance with the CA typology I established by Kenworthy (1984). Seed house’s (2005) framework for CA, adapted from Kenworthy (1984), was employed to aEnalyze the audio-recorded data. This process involved several systematic steps. First, the Ldata underwent an unmotivated examination, where the transcripts were reviewed withoutC reference to any specific research objectives, allowing for an open-ended exploration of the cIontent. Second, an inductive analysis was conducted to identify T instances of the phenomenon under investigation. During this phase, the transcripts were analyzed R with the research questions in mind, and relevant sections aligned with the study’s objectives were highlighted. The thirdA step involved identifying regularities and patterns in the data. This was achieved by categorizing the transcripts according to the types of repair initiations, their functions, and the corresponding repair types. The observational notes on nonverbal cues were also integrated to provide a richer and more nuanced analysis. In this final step, the findings were critically linked to relevant existing literature to offer a comprehensive analysis and deeper understanding of the phenomenon. 4 Results The rest of the study focuses on the verbal and non-verbal repair initiation strategies ESL students and teachers employ to achieve intersubjectivity in classroom discourse. (.1)(cupping the hand behind ear)’. The student responded to the repair initiation by repeating the problematic part, saying ‘Big land’. This repetition is an attempt to address the difficulty in understanding. The teacher in Line 7 acknowledges the repair by confirming the corrected version, saying, ‘Big Land’. This signifies the successful resolution of the trouble source, indicating that the repair sequence has been effective in achieving mutual understanding. Furthermore, in Extract 6, the teacher employed cupping the hand behind the ear in addition to the verbal utterance to initiate repair. Although the repair could have been initiated without the paralinguistic feature (cupping the hand behind ear), the teacher may have wanted to cater for students who may have difficulties in hearing. 4.2 Function of Repair Initiations ARTICLE IN PRESS Interactional functions The findings revealed that the interlocutors initiated repair for diverse interactional effects. In this regard, they initiated repair in order to promote understanding (clarification and disambiguation), manage interaction (turn-taking, participation) and regulate sequential order (delaying progress for comprehension) of classroom interaction. For instance in Extract 1, the teacher’s use of the prolonged “Huh?” and the follow-up question “Losing what?” functions as a clarification request. Although the student used the word “loosely,” the teacher hears or interprets it as “losing,” likely triggering confusion. This moment marks an important interactive function of repair initiation: promoting understanding through clarification and disambiguation. The teacher leans forward, signalling heightened attentiveness, and seeks to resolve ambiguity, which is crucial for mutual comprehension in classroom communication. Again, in Extract 3, the teacher asks the student ‘Francis:::: who::?’ after the student had mentioned his name ‘Francis(.2)Anaba’. This teacher makes this request for clarification in order to obtain referential specificity for the name mentioned, helping to enhanceS the flow of the interaction. S S2 in Extract 1, steps in to offer clarification: “They were walking loosely from Bawku to Bolga”. This restatement is delivered moreE assertively, with a slight lean back in posture, suggesting confidence and an attempt toR correct both the phrasing and the misunderstanding. The student’s intervention demoPnstrates how repair initiation can stimulate peer-supported meaning-making, encouraging lear ners to collaboratively negotiate meaning and N resolve confusion, a key pedagogical strategy in communicative classrooms. The teacher Extract 1 again then transitions smoothly by pointinIg to another student and asking, “So (.) what (.) what will be the adverb E of this…?” This interaction marks a shift from repair to extension, using the repair sequencLe as a springboard to deepen grammatical understanding. C The teacher’s pacing and repetition of “what” functions as a mechanism for managing interaction I and turn-taking, giving the student time to focus and respond. The use of gesture and gaze direction T toward the pointed student further organizes turn allocation, ensuring active participation and equal R distribution of classroom talk. Additionally, the initiation in Extract 1 serves to regulate sequential A order in the lesson. The teacher temporarily suspends content progression to ensure the class has fully understood both the linguistic form “loosely” and its grammatical category “adverb of manner” before moving on. This delay supports comprehension and provides an opportunity to consolidate learning, a critical pedagogical move in language instruction. It also accommodates the speaker processing needs of both teacher and students. The pause, the slow phrasing of the question, and the repetition offer learners a chance to organize their thoughts and recall relevant grammatical knowledge. Pedagogical functions In some other instances of the use of repair, the goal was seen to be pedagogical in nature. In these instances, the repair was seen to have been initiated with the aim of supporting the teaching and learning process beyond the maintenance of interactional flow. Precisely, these repair initiations are aimed at identifying/correcting errors in concepts being learnt or reinforcing knowledge of such concepts. Extracts 1 and 2 provide compelling insights into how repair initiation serves important pedagogical functions in second language learning environments. In both cases, repair initiation is not merely a reaction to confusion or error but is deeply integrated into instructional strategy, particularly in ways that support learner participation and accommodate learners’ ARTICLE IN PRESS cognitive processing needs. In Extract 1, when the teacher misinterprets the student’s sentence, mistaking “loosely” for “losing”, the resulting repair sequence becomes a platform for collaborative clarification. Another student steps in to reformulate the original utterance more clearly: “They were walking loosely from Bawku to Bolga.” This peer-led clarification demonstrates learning through participation, where students are not passive recipients of correction but active co-constructors of meaning. The teacher builds on this moment by shifting the discussion from contextual use to grammatical form, asking for the “adverb of this.” Thus, the repair sequence does more than resolve confusion it transitions into an opportunity for explicit metalinguistic reflection. The interaction creates a natural flow from communication to grammar instruction, guided by student input. In Extract 2, the repair sequence revolves around a student’s attempt to engage with the teacher’s explanation of a topic sentence. The student proposes an alternative: “Can we use ‘importance of eggs’?” This moment is particularly pedagogically rich because it reflects a student testing their understanding against academic writinSg norms. The teacher’s repair initiation “You mean, we should use… important of eggs as topic S sentence?” serves not as a rejection, but as a candidate understanding, a way of clarifying what E the student meant. The student confirms, prompting the teacher to deliver a principled explanation R about topic sentences needing to be drawn directly from the text. This moment supports learning P by inviting the student to participate in the negotiation of academic language and understand genre- specific conventions. The interaction thus reflects a pedagogical commitment to learning through N dialogic clarification, not just correction. In Extract 1 and 2 also respond to or reflect the processing I needs of learners, particularly around memo ry, attention, and conceptual clarity. In Extract 1, the initial misunderstanding may result froEm phonological similarity between “loosely” and “losing,” a common area of confLusion in second language learning. The teacher’s repetition C and request for clarification serve to draw the class’s attention to the form and meaning of the utterance. Moreover, by restatiIng the sentence and shifting the focus to grammatical analysis T “what will be the adverb of this?”, the teacher helps students encode the correct R form more robustly in memory. The brief pause and repetition in phrasing “what (.) what A will be the adverb…” also suggest the teacher is managing their own processing as well, ensuring the question is clearly framed before turn allocation. These interactional features show how classroom discourse is attuned to real-time cognitive demands. Social functions Some repairs were also initiated in ways that achieved social goals beyond pedagogical ones. In this respect, the initiation had undertones of power and face negotiation. In this regard, some initiations had undertones of the teachers’ assertion of authority. For instance, in Extract 1, the teacher’s pause (0.2) and pointing (“So (.) what…”) practically control the interaction pace, while in Extract 2, the rejection (“No, anytime…”) reinforces the teacher’s epistemic authority. There were also instances of the use of repair initiations to preserve face. Extract 3 shows the teacher pre-empting face-threat (“I’m new…do not worry”) alongside an elicitation of a name repetition, while Extract 6 (“Do we have a goat that is red?”) suggests the use of humour to soften corrections in ways that preserve student dignity. Similarly, there were instances of the teachers’ use of light- hearted tones (e.g. laughter in Extract 6) or encouragement (e.g. ‘that’s good’ in Extract 4) to maintain a positive classroom climate. These instances illustrate that repair initiations are not merely mechanisms for correcting errors and negotiating meaning but are also crucial in managing ARTICLE IN PRESS interpersonal relations and maintaining social equilibrium in the classroom. In effect, they demonstrate the teachers’ roles as instructional guides and facilitators of a supportive, inclusive learning environment. Discussion This study aimed at exploring the repair initiation strategies employed in ESL classrooms in Ghana. The findings presented in the preceding section indicate that ESL interlocutors in Ghana employ four verbal repair initiation and two nonverbal repair initiation strategies to achieve intersubjectivity in the classroom. This study offers genuine novelty in its identification and categorization of both oral and nonverbal repair initiation strategies within Ghanaian ESL classroom discourse an area underexplored in existing conversation analytic literature. While prior studies (e.g. Aleksius, 2021; Atar & Seedhouse, 2018) have predominantly focused on naturalistic or L2 conversations in non-instructional contexts, this study contributes fresh empirical evidence S from a formal educational setting in Ghana, where interactional norms are shaped by both S linguistic and cultural specificities. E R A key contribution lies in the finding that four oral and two nonverbal repair initiation strategies P are systematically employed to maintain intersubjectivity. The integration of embodied cues such as cupping the ear alongside verbal repair strategNies reflects a multimodal interactional competence that is underrepresented in classroom-based studies. While Mortensen (2016) and Balaman (2017) I examined nonverbal cues in broader interac tional contexts, this study contextualizes them within pedagogical activities, showing their funEction not only in expressing comprehension difficulty but also in eliciting attention and activeL listening from students. Moreover, the absence of repair initiators like “sorry” or “WhCat did you say?” common in Western or Asian datasets demonstrates how repair resourcIes are locally contingent and culturally filtered (Aleksius, 2021; T Golato & Golato, 2015; Hayashi & Kim, 2015; Jan & Saad, 2018). This divergence suggests that R Ghanaian classroom interaction draws from a culturally grounded repertoire, which does not merely reproduce WesAtern L2 classroom models but modifies them to suit the interactional ethos of the local environment. Another novel contribution is the emphasis on candidate understanding as a tool not only for resolving comprehension issues but for stimulating learner engagement and prompting elaboration. Unlike prior studies that primarily treat candidate understandings as repair initiators (Aleksius, 2021; Atar et al, 2022; Atar & Seedhouse, 2018; Waring et al., 2016), this study illustrates how they are used by students and teachers alike to co-construct knowledge, thus performing a dual pedagogical and interactional function. Further distinctive feature is the use of relational framing during repair sequences. For example, in the exchange where a teacher forgets a student’s name, the teacher prefaces the repair with a self-deprecating explanation: “I am new in this class, so I am not all that familiar with your name”. Here, the repair is not presented as a demand for accuracy but as a relational act that maintains the student’s face and reinforces rapport. This pattern deviates from traditional CA models that treat repair primarily as a mechanism for resolving trouble in speaking, hearing, or understanding (e.g. Kääntä, 2010; Mortensen, 2016; Schegloff et al., 1977; Sert, 2015; Waring, 2021). Instead, Ghanaian teachers appear to embed repair within a broader ARTICLE IN PRESS framework of communal politeness and face work, reflecting indigenous communicative norms where social harmony is prioritized. Additionally, the use of humour and group affiliation during repair initiation provides further insight into the local adaptation of CA norms. For instance, in the "Red goat" sequence, a teacher’s ironic question “Do we have a goat that is red?” elicits shared laughter among the students. This interactional moment highlights how laughter and humour are strategically used to manage errors in a non-threatening way (Clift, 2016; Atar et al, 2021; Dingemanse & Enfield, 2015). Rather than creating embarrassment, the repair initiation becomes an opportunity for bonding and shared understanding. This challenges more conventional views of classroom repair as face-threatening. In addition, the findings extend the literature by demonstrating how repair initiation in Ghanaian classrooms serve layered purposes, interactional (clarifying ambiguity), pedagogical (correcting and reinforcing knowledge), and social (managing face and authority). While the interactional function of repair is well documented (e.g. Schegloff et al., 1977; Walsh, 2012), this study shows that teachers strategiScally explore repair initiation to assert epistemic authority, maintain discipline, and structure tuSrn-taking, all of which underscore the intersection of linguistic repair and classroom power dynamics (Atar, 2016; Liebscher & E Dailey–O’Cain, 2003). This study challenges the assumption that repair mechanisms are R universally uniform across instructional settings. Instead, it highlights how Ghanaian classroom P practices offer a context-sensitive model of repair, one that enriches existing theoretical understandings by demonstrating how culturallyN embedded multimodal repair mechanisms operate within institutional discourse. I Implications for Policy and Practice E L This study enriches the literature on teacher-led interactions in senior high school ESL classrooms C in Ghana, focusing on underexplored classroom discourse and repair practices. It addresses the I gap in research on how teacheTrs handle communication breakdowns during classroom interactions, and how their approach toR addressing this conversational breakdown functions beyond the primary goal of enhancing inAteractional flow. By examining repair initiation strategies (e.g. WH- interrogatives, requests for clarification, leaning forward, cupping the hand behind the ear), the study highlights the various ways in which they manifest. This helps in improving teacher awareness of these strategies and how linguistic and paralinguistic repair mechanisms may be employed to effectively manage classroom interaction. Moreover, the findings point to how teachers could employ repair to enhance the achievement of teaching and learning objectives and the extent to which teacher and student roles and authority may be evidenced in the repair initiation attempt. These findings further point to the possibility of capitalising on repair to improve classroom productivity and enhance social relationships in educational contexts. However, it must be noted that the overuse of repair in the classroom may engender negative outcomes such as limiting effective classroom interaction and heightening the levels of anxiety in students. Caution is, therefore, necessary to ensure that repair is initiated judiciously with a focus on creating supportive classroom environments instead of overemphasising correction. With this, teachers should strive for balance, using repair selectively to enhance learning without discouraging student participation. ARTICLE IN PRESS Conclusion The objectives of the study were to explore repair initiation strategies and examine their functions in teacher-led ESL classroom interactions guided by CA in its methodological approach in senior high schools in the Upper East region of Ghana. The study uncovered six different types of repair initiation with four verbal and two nonverbal repair initiation strategies through the micro-analytic examination of the data. The four types of verbal repair initiation are open-class or unspecified, checking understanding, partial repeat plus WH-interrogatives, request to speak up/request for repetition, while the non-verbal repair initiation strategies include leaning forward and cupping the hand behind the ear. The study has underscored that proficient and inexperienced language users initiate the repair process. Notably, the majority of students were observed using open-class initiation, while teachers employed other types of repair initiations, encompassing partial repeat plus WH-interrogatives, understanding checkers, and request to speak up/request for repetition. Finally, leaning forward and cupping the hand behind the ear have been shown to contribute to S repair initiating in classroom discourse. Consequently, this study adds to the understanding of S repair practices in the classroom and the use of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena in repair E initiation. JSON: Name: multimodal_repair_esl_ghana Title: Multimodal conversation analysis of repair initiation effects on repair completion in Ghanaian ESL classroom interactions Short Hypothesis: Multimodal repair initiation (simultaneous verbal plus nonverbal cues) increases the probability of successful repair completion compared to verbal-only repair initiation in ESL classroom interactions. Related Work: Conversation analysis has established taxonomy and sequential organization of other-initiated repair and self-repair; prior classroom CA work documented teacher-initiated and student-initiated repair formats (open requests, restricted requests, partial repeats) and has begun to note embodied resources (leaning forward, cupping ear). Existing studies are predominantly descriptive and cross-sectional, often focused on non-institutional or Western contexts, with limited quantitative comparisons between modality conditions. Work on multimodality in repair is emergent but underpowered: it identifies embodied cues but rarely measures their causal association with repair outcomes, controls weakly for classroom clustering, and seldom tests teacher-vs-student initiator effects or disaggregates specific gestures. There is also a scarcity of reproducible annotated datasets from non-Western ESL classrooms, limiting cross-context validation. In short, current approaches provide strong qualitative descriptions but lack controlled, quantitative tests of whether and how multimodal repair initiations causally affect repair success or pedagogical outcomes. Abstract: This project investigates whether multimodal repair initiations—verbal repair initiations produced together with embodied cues such as leaning forward or cupping the ear—increase the likelihood of successful repair completion in Ghanaian senior high school ESL classrooms. Using conversation-analytic micro-transcription and systematic multimodal annotation of naturally occurring classroom recordings, the study operationalizes repair initiation types and measures repair outcomes (completion, time-to-repair, and immediate uptake). The main contribution is a reproducible, mixed-method pipeline combining manual multimodal annotation, hierarchical statistical modeling, and ablation comparisons to quantify the effect of multimodality on repair success while controlling for initiator role, class size, and student proficiency. Expected outcomes include (1) empirical estimates of the effect size of multimodal cues on repair completion, (2) an annotated dataset and annotation schema for classroom repair, and (3) evidence-informed recommendations for classroom interactional practice and teacher training. Results will clarify the functional contribution of embodied resources to communicative repair in a non-Western ESL instructional context. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = 52 hours of audio–video recordings from Ghanaian senior high school ESL lessons (as described in the source); augment with minimum additional 48 hours of similarly recorded ESL lessons from comparable schools to achieve ~100 hours; extract and timestamp all repair-initiating turns producing a target set of repair instances (expected target >=600 repair instances). Annotation: develop a multimodal annotation schema labeling (a) initiator (teacher/student), (b) initiation type (open-class, restricted request, partial repeat+WH, request-for-repetition), (c) nonverbal cue presence (leaning forward, cupping ear, gaze, head tilt), (d) modality class (verbal-only, nonverbal-only, multimodal), (e) repair outcome (successful completion within two turns: yes/no), (f) time-to-repair (seconds), (g) class-level covariates (class size, proficiency level). Inter-annotator reliability: compute Cohen's kappa for categorical labels and ICC for continuous measures; require kappa>=0.75. Baselines: (1) verbal-only baseline (all verbal-only initiation instances), (2) qualitative CA baseline (manual labeling without multimodal coding), (3) automated acoustic-only classifier predicting repair success using prosodic features. Evaluation metrics: primary = repair completion rate (binary) and odds ratio; secondary = time-to-repair (median seconds), immediate uptake rate, post-lesson retention gain (pre/post mini-quiz where available). Statistical analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression predicting repair success with fixed effects: modality (multimodal vs verbal-only), initiator role, initiation type, pause length before initiation, utterance length, class size, proficiency; random intercepts for teacher and class; report odds ratios, 95% CIs, p-values. Additional models: mixed-effects linear regression for time-to-repair (log-transformed). Ablation studies: (A) restrict dataset to teacher-initiated instances only; (B) restrict to student-initiated only; (C) remove each nonverbal cue type in turn (lean forward removed, cupping removed) to estimate individual cue contributions; (D) compare multimodal vs nonverbal-only. Robustness checks: propensity score stratification on class-level covariates; permutation test of modality labels; sensitivity analysis excluding high-leverage classes. Power analysis: target >=600 repair instances to detect an odds ratio of 1.5 with alpha=0.05 and power=0.8 given intra-class correlation of 0.05. Reproducibility: provide annotation manual, de-identified timestamps, model code, and aggregated results; do not publish raw video without consent. Risk Factors and Limitations: Observer and recording effects may alter natural interaction and nonverbal behavior; annotation subjectivity and multimodal label ambiguity may reduce reliability despite training; video/audio quality variability can prevent detection of subtle nonverbal cues; sample is geographically and institutionally constrained (Upper East Region, Ghana) limiting external generalization to other cultural/educational contexts; observational design limits causal inference due to potential unmeasured confounds (teacher style, classroom management, socio-economic variables); clustering by teacher/class reduces effective sample size and requires hierarchical models; low frequency of some gesture types (e.g., cupping) may reduce statistical power for disaggregated analyses; ethical/privacy constraints restrict sharing of raw multimodal recordings, complicating replication; automated feature extraction may perform poorly on noisy classroom audio and varied camera angles, limiting scaled analyses.
